newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION - No global money policy upturn - F.Schroeder.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - No global money policy upturn - F.Schroeder.

text.p: By Frank Schroeder, Trinkaus Capital Management
As a result of sluggish economic development and growing "euro" scepticism due to the greater likelihood of a large monetary union, the external value of the D-mark has declined sharply.

The Japanese currency, in turn, is suffering from unsolved structural problems and an extremely low interest rate level. At the same time, the central banks in Great Britain, the Netherlands, and recently also in the USA have shifted to a more restrictive monetary policy. Against this background, the question necessarily arises whether a trend reversal is under way in the monetary policy of the large industrialised nations.

In view of currently low inflation rates (except in Great Britain), a change of direction in monetary policy is primarily explicable by reference to rising inflationary expectations, whose fulfilment central bankers seek to prevent.

Globally increasing competitive pressure, visible rationalisation success, and wage restraint compelled by greater job uncertainty will not allow a relapse to the inflation level of the l97Os and 1980s. Nevertheless, serious global and regional threats to the currently calm price climate should not be overlooked.

These undoubtedly include the positive prospects for economic development (in Europe, not least due to the foreseeable easing of fiscal policy reins after 1998), the latest revaluation of exchange rate parities, the monetary policy implications of EMU, and the coming increase of indirect taxes. According to the consensus forecast, 1998 inflation expectations for Germany, Great Britain, and Japan are 0.5-1.0 percentage points higher than 1996 inflation rates; only in the case of Italy is a significantly lower inflation rate forecast (-1.3 percentage points).
The monetary fuel appears already assured by the abundant supply of liquidity in the past; it is well known that prices of goods only react to changes of the money supply aggregate at a time lag.

Concretely, we expect in the first half of 1997 further key interest rate hikes by 25 to 50 basis points in the USA and Great Britain. In the course of the year, one more interest rate step could follow. Despite the pronounced weakness of the yen and associated trade policy frictions, we regard a reversal of trend in Japanese monetary policy as likely only if the economic situation stabilises at the end of 1997.

In contrast, a tightening of monetary policy in Germany (manifested in the discount and lombard rates) and France may be expected at the earliest in the first half of 1998, when expected growth acceleration will make employment effects likely and thus open up room for passing on price increases.

German monetary policy, in particular, is already operating largely in the shadow of EMU. With a view to domestic and foreign acceptance of the euro, the Bundesbank must be concerned to combat expectations of inflation and devaluation already in advance of the single currency in order to give the European Central Bank the greatest possible credibility from the outset.
This necessarily includes attaining its own current inflation and money supply goals, especially since the concept of money supply control is also to be established at the European level.

Despite the latest weakness of the mark and current deviation of money supply growth from its target range, an increase of the German discount and lombard rates in 1997 is nevertheless unlikely, in our opinion.

In addition to weak domestic demand, declining unit labour costs, and slowing money supply growth in the course of the year, we regard political reasons as also decisive for this. Budgets deficits, especially in Italy, Portugal, Belgium, and Ireland, react sensitively to changes in the interest rate level, so that efforts at viable consolidation of European state finances could be easily thwarted.

Only a further significant devaluation of the D-mark, e.g. at the six-year high between DM 1.78 and 1.85 per US dollar, could make the Bundesbank nervous. In that case, an early tightening (e.g. by raising tender rates) cannot be ruled out.

A further aspect relevant for the Bundesbank's special preventative responsibility for the stability of the euro lies dormant in the future capacity for monetary policy on the part of the "Club Med" countries.

In case of an on-schedule participation as of 1 January 1999, considerable manoeuvring room for interest rate reduction will exist at the latest from May 1998, since the Mark will increasingly lose its anchor function in the period leading up to the commencement of the monetary union.

By comparison, the interest rates for three-month money exceeded the German level by 2.6 to 4.1 percentage points at the end of March. In contrast, the French central bank may be expected to fulfil its psychological responsibility for the euro's future stability although there is an existing preference towards stimulating the economy by means of monetary and currency policy.

Concretely, that would mean that it will waive its growing monetary policy autonomy and not allow its key interest rates to fall below the German level. Conversely, however, this should also place a ceiling on the Bundesbank's room for action. If, on the other hand, the "Club Med" countries are not among the starting participants in EMU, then devaluation expectations will also force the Mediterranean central banks to adopt a more restrictive course.

In that case, the Bundesbank may be expected to step more gently on the monetary brakes in the course of 1998." /////Dr. Frank Schroeder is a bond market analyst at Trinkaus Capital Management. The views expressed are those of the author alone and not those of Reuters.
